passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 4.6.6 Contract manager
passages.text: The contract manager is accountable to the senior business owner for managing the day-to-day delivery of a contract, including production and maintenance of the contract management plan (see 5.3.6).

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 4.6.5 Senior business owner
passages.text: The commercial functional standard places a senior business owner above each contract or group of related contracts. That person owns the justification for the contract, is accountable for parts of its governance and management, and makes sure commercial and other specialists stay involved across the whole commercial life cycle.
passages.anchor: own the justification for the contract(s)

passages.locator: Contract Management Principles, principle 2
passages.text: Be clear about accountability, roles and responsibilities. Ensure contract ownership, management processes and governance mechanisms are clear with defined roles and responsibilities at appropriate levels of seniority.

passages.locator: Contract Management Principles, principle 4
passages.text: Adopt a differentiated approach based on risk; distinguish between tactical and strategic contracts, direct the most/strongest resource to contracts where the risks and rewards are highest.

passages.locator: Contract Management Framework Summary, Area 1: Planning & Governance, item 1
passages.text: Contract ownership, management processes and governance mechanisms are clear with defined roles and responsibilities.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), The Fundamentals: Role of Contract Manager, p.4
passages.text: The World Bank's guidance treats appointing a contract manager for each contract as good practice.
passages.anchor: Good practice requires that a Contract Manager is appointed for every contract.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Introduction: Purpose, p.1
passages.text: The guidance reminds its reader that a contract is managed according to its own terms.
passages.anchor: It should be kept in mind that contracts shall be managed in accordance with the contract.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed. (Sept 2025), Section V para 5.97, p.34
passages.text: The Regulations give contract management one aim: that every party meets what it owes under the contract.
passages.anchor: The aim of contract management is to ensure that all parties meet their obligations.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed. (Sept 2025), Annex XI para 2.1, p.101
passages.text: The Regulations call for contract management that is planned, carried out, monitored and evaluated systematically, so that performance is optimised and risks are managed.
passages.anchor: Effective contract management requires systematic and efficient planning, execution, monitoring, and evaluation to optimize performance while managing risks

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 12, p.68
passages.text: All outsourced services should be built on a robust contractual relationship overseen by an appropriately qualified contract manager with a clear operational understanding of the contract.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 12, p.68
passages.text: How a contract will be managed is a key strategic decision that needs adequate consideration early in the procurement process and shall be reflected in the contractual agreement.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.16(21)
passages.text: The accounting officer of a procuring entity and any officer to whom responsibility is delegated are responsible and accountable for any actions taken or omitted to be taken either in compliance with or in contravention of this Act.

passages.locator: Contract Management Principles, principle 1
passages.text: Make sure that adequate resource is identified and appointed well before award of contracts and that there is an effective handover or transition from sourcing to contract management.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.2 Contract management plan
passages.text: A contract management plan should be established that defines the roles and the responsibilities of each party, and should be reviewed periodically throughout the life of the contract.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.2 Contract management plan
passages.text: The plan should be produced by the contract manager (see 4.6.6) and be approved by the senior business owner (see 4.6.5).

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.1 Mobilisation
passages.text: The commercial functional standard treats mobilisation as the start of delivery. Simple, low cost contracts may need no commercial specialist support, while for more complex contracts the roles for managing the contract (senior business owner, contract manager, commercial specialists) should be confirmed during mobilisation.
passages.anchor: for more complex contracts the roles and responsibilities in managing the contract should be confirmed during mobilisation

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 12, p.68
passages.text: Immediately following contract award and prior to the contract start date, mobilisation is a key phase in setting up an outsourcing project for success.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex XI para 2.3, p.101
passages.text: Under the Regulations a contract management plan is drafted while the contract is being created and finished by the time it is signed.
passages.anchor: A Contract Management Plan is developed during contract creation and completed at the time the contract is signed.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex I para 3.7
passages.text: For the contracts its procurement strategy identifies, the Borrower prepares a contract management plan that sets key performance indicators and milestone events.
passages.anchor: for contracts identified in the PPSD, the Borrower shall develop a Contract Management Plan with key performance indicators and milestone events.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex XI para 3.1(a) to (j), pp.101 to 102
passages.text: Under the World Bank Regulations a contract management plan typically summarises: identified risks and their mitigation; key contacts, roles and the authorisations each party has set up; communication and reporting; local labour monitoring; key terms; milestones and the critical path with payment procedures; key deliverables kept up to date for change orders; KPIs and how they are measured; variation and change control; and record keeping.
passages.anchor: contract variation/change control mechanisms; and

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Preparing a CMP, item 1, p.11
passages.text: The guidance asks the contract manager to confirm at the start that each party has put its authorisations and delegations in place, since a contracting decision is valid and enforceable only when the person taking it holds the authority to take it.
passages.anchor: ensure that each party has established the necessary authorizations and delegations for its personnel at the beginning of the contract as this is an important prerequisite to ensuring that all contracting decisions are valid and enforceable

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Contract Start-up, pp.13 to 14
passages.text: At start-up the employer checks that any performance security matches the contract in amount, validity and wording, verifies doubtful securities with the issuing institution before paying an advance, makes the advance on time once an acceptable advance payment guarantee is in, and checks that required insurances are in place.
passages.anchor: Check that the amount, validity and text are in accordance with the contract document

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Consulting Services: Kick-off Meeting, p.82
passages.text: A kick-off meeting should at least introduce the parties and their roles, set communication and reporting procedures, walk through the contract documents and payment schedules, agree escalation routes for bottlenecks, and confirm that everyone shares the same understanding of obligations, timelines and risks.
passages.anchor: define escalation procedures to resolve critical situations or bottlenecks

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Consulting Services: Kick-off Meeting, item 3, p.82
passages.text: At a consulting kick-off meeting the guidance lists a walk through the contract documents, so that everyone understands the key provisions, which document takes priority over which, the conditions, the terms of reference, the payment schedule and the milestones.
passages.anchor: reviewing the contract documents to ensure everyone understands the key provisions, the priority and inter-correlation of contract documents, conditions of contract, TOR, payment schedules and covenants, implementation milestones (deliverables, reports etc.)

passages.locator: Contract Management Framework Summary, Area 8: Contract Development, item 10
passages.text: Contract management staff understand the contractual terms including contract extension (services and duration), termination warranties, indemnities, insurance, security and confidentiality and dispute resolution.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex VIII para 3.2, p.87
passages.text: Under a lump-sum contract the contractor or consultant performs the defined scope for a fixed contract amount.
passages.anchor: Under a lump-sum contract, the contractor/Consultant agrees to perform the scope of services for a fixed contract amount.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex VIII para 3.6, p.88
passages.text: A unit price contract states estimated quantities and a unit price for each item, and pays the quantities actually delivered at those unit prices.
passages.anchor: This type of contract is based on estimated quantities of items and contractual unit prices for each of these items and is paid on the actual quantities and contractual unit prices.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex VIII para 3.4, p.87
passages.text: A performance-based contract ties payment to measured outputs that meet functional needs of quality, quantity and reliability.
passages.anchor: In a performance-based contract, the payments are not made for inputs but for measured outputs that aim at satisfying functional needs in terms of quality, quantity, and reliability.

passages.locator: Risk Allocation and Pricing Approaches guidance note (Jan 2026), Appendix II: Fixed Price, p.34
passages.text: The pricing guidance ties fixed price to fixed scope. If the scope floats or is still unknown, a fixed price does not fit, and where base prices cannot be estimated at all a cost plus approach may be the only option.
passages.anchor: In this case, cost plus pricing approaches may be the only option.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.16(28)
passages.text: Nigeria's Public Procurement Act requires every procurement contract to carry warranties: durability of goods, requisite skill in service provision, and genuine materials and inputs in execution. Reading the warranty clause is part of reading any Nigerian public contract.
passages.anchor: All procurement contracts shall contain warranties for durability of goods,

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.16(27)
passages.text: The values in procurement documents shall be stated in Nigerian currency

passages.locator: FIDIC Conditions of Contract (as embedded in World Bank SPD General Conditions): concept only
passages.text: Many international works contracts, including those built on World Bank standard documents, use FIDIC general conditions with project specific particular conditions. A reader works through the agreement, the particular conditions and the general conditions in the order the contract itself sets, and checks the role given to the Engineer or Employer's Representative.

passages.locator: AIPN model contracts: concept only
passages.text: AIPN publishes model contracts, such as its model joint operating and farmout agreements, that many upstream parties adapt for their own deals. A contract manager reads the version the parties actually signed, since elections and amendments in a model form change its effect from deal to deal.

passages.locator: LOGIC standard contracts: concept only
passages.text: LOGIC standard contracts are industry forms used on the UK continental shelf for offshore services, construction and supply. A contract manager reads the edition and any agreed amendments in the signed contract before relying on a clause.

passages.locator: Procurement Act 2023, s.52(1)
passages.text: Before entering into a public contract with an estimated value of more than £5 million, a contracting authority must set at least three key performance indicators in respect of the contract.

passages.locator: Procurement Act 2023, s.52(4)
passages.text: A “key performance indicator” is a factor or measure against which a supplier’s performance of a contract can be assessed during the life-cycle of the contract.

passages.locator: Guidance: Key Performance Indicators (Procurement Act 2023), para 10
passages.text: The duty to set at least three KPIs falls away where the authority considers that performance could not appropriately be assessed through KPIs; the guidance gives a one-off delivery of off-the-shelf goods as an example.
passages.anchor: This might include, for example, where the contract is for a one-off delivery of or off-the-shelf

passages.locator: Guidance: Key Performance Indicators (Procurement Act 2023), para 14
passages.text: at least once in every twelve month period during the lifetime of the contract and on termination, assess the supplier’s performance against those KPIs

passages.locator: Guidance: Key Performance Indicators (Procurement Act 2023), para 15 and table (regulation 39(5))
passages.text: Published KPI assessments use five ratings set by regulation: Good (meeting or exceeding the KPI), Approaching target, Requires improvement (below the KPI), Inadequate (significantly below the KPI) and Other (none of those descriptions fits).
passages.anchor: Inadequate Performance is significantly below the KPI

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 5: KPIs and baselines, p.39
passages.text: having too many KPIs (i.e. more than 10 to 15 per service) will lead to overcomplicated contracts and ambiguity with suppliers.

passages.locator: Contract Management Principles, principle 7
passages.text: Use a balanced scorecard to measure ‘hard’ data such as KPI performance alongside ‘soft’ measures e.g. customer satisfaction and relationship management, with a focus on achievement of outcomes.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), KPIs: Good Practice, item 10, p.94
passages.text: When a KPI is missed, the guidance expects the underlying cause to be found and the problems dealt with through an action plan.
passages.anchor: If a KPI is not met, the underlying cause should be identified, and issues or bottlenecks addressed in an action plan

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex XI para 2.4, p.101
passages.text: Where they are needed, the Regulations set key performance indicators to confirm that the contractor performs satisfactorily and meets the requirements of the contract.
passages.anchor: Where required Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) are set to ensure that contractor performance is satisfactory, contract requirements are met

passages.locator: Procurement Act 2023, s.68(2)
passages.text: Any sum due to be paid under the public contract by the contracting authority must be paid before the end of the period of 30 days beginning with

passages.locator: Guidance: Electronic Invoicing and Payment (Procurement Act 2023), para 7
passages.text: Under the UK Act's implied payment term, payment is due within 30 days of the day the invoice is received, or by the later due date shown on the invoice, provided the invoice is valid and undisputed. The same terms are implied into public sub-contracts.
passages.anchor: within 30 days of the day the invoice is received

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Payment Information (Procurement Act 2023), para 3
passages.text: a contracting authority must publish specified information about payments of more than £30,000 (including VAT) made by the authority under public contracts

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.37(2)
passages.text: Any payment due after more than sixty days from the date of the submission of the invoice, valuation certificate and confirmation or authentication by the Ministry, Extra-Ministerial Office, Government Agency, Parastatal or Corporation shall be deem a delayed payment.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.37(3) and (4)
passages.text: All delayed payments shall attract interest at the rate specified in the contract document. (4) All contracts shall include terms, specifying the interest for late payment of more than sixty days.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.35(1)
passages.text: a mobilization fee of not more than 15% may be paid to a supplier or contractor supported by the following

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.35(2)
passages.text: Once a mobilization fee has been paid to any supplier or contractor, no further payment shall be made to the supplier or contractor without an interim performance certificate issued in accordance with the contract agreement.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.36
passages.text: The provision of a Performance Guarantee shall be a precondition for the award of any procurement contract upon which any mobilization fee is to be paid, provided however it shall not be less than 10% of the contract value in any case or an amount equivalent to the mobilization fee requested by the supplier or contractor whichever is higher.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.16(12) and (13)
passages.text: Procuring entities must keep both file and electronic records of all procurement proceedings each financial year. The printed Act gives the retention period as "often years from the date of the award", which looks like a misprint, so the period should be confirmed against another official copy before a number is taught. Copies go to the Bureau not later than 3 months after the end of the financial year.
passages.anchor: the procurement records shall be maintained for a period often years from the date of the award. (13) Copies of all procurement records shall be transmitted to the Bureau not later than 3 months

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.38(5)
passages.text: The records and documents maintained by procuring entities on procurement shall be made available for inspection by the Bureau, an investigator appointed by the Bureau and the Auditor-General upon request

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.4 Payments to suppliers
passages.text: Payments should be audited periodically to ensure they reflect the contract terms and service levels received from suppliers.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex IX para 2.14
passages.text: For works, the Regulations provide that a contract may, where appropriate, allow for a mobilisation advance, for advances against the plant and materials the contractor brings, for regular payments as progress is made, and for a reasonable retention that is released once the contractor has met its obligations.
passages.anchor: In appropriate cases contracts for Works shall provide, for mobilization advances, advances on contractor’s equipment and materials, regular progress payments, and reasonable retention amounts to be released upon the contractor’s compliance with its obligations under the contract.

passages.locator: Kraljic, P. (1983) 'Purchasing must become supply management', Harvard Business Review 61(5): concept only
passages.text: Kraljic's portfolio idea sorts purchased items by two questions: how much the item affects profit, and how risky or complex its supply market is. Items then fall into four groups (strategic, bottleneck, leverage and non-critical), and each group gets its own purchasing and relationship approach.

passages.locator: WB PPSD Guidance (Aug 2025), Tool: Supply Positioning Model, p.17
passages.text: The World Bank's supply positioning model places each procurement by its relative supply risk and its value.
passages.anchor: It simply categorizes specific procurements based on their relative supply risk and value.

passages.locator: WB PPSD Guidance (Aug 2025), Figure IV and Table IV, pp.17 to 18
passages.text: The World Bank's supply positioning model has four quadrants: Strategic Security (low cost and strategically important), Strategic Critical (high cost, few suppliers), Tactical Acquisition (routine and low value, with many suppliers) and Tactical Advantage (high cost and low risk, with many suppliers). The guidance usually counts a contract as high cost when its estimate reaches 1 percent of the project's total estimated procurement cost.
passages.anchor: any contract that is 1 percent or more of the estimated total Project procurement costs

passages.locator: WB PPSD Guidance (Aug 2025), Tool: Supplier Preferencing, Figure VI, p.28 (detailed in Annex A)
passages.text: Supplier preferencing places the buyer in one of four segments (Development, Core, Nuisance, Exploitable) using two dimensions: the value of the buyer's business to the supplier and how attractive that business is. A buyer that suppliers see as core or worth developing tends to get more effort from them.
passages.anchor: Development Core Nuisance Exploitable

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Introduction, definitions note 6, p.8
passages.text: These can be identified using the Cabinet Office Contract Tiering Tool, which considers factors such as the potential impact of service failure; service continuity; the speed and ease of switching suppliers; and the contract value.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 6.3 Supplier relationship management
passages.text: Suppliers should be segmented according to their commercial and business impact.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 6.2 (supplier relationships)
passages.text: The commercial functional standard accepts that some suppliers need no relationship management at all, typically where the goods, works or services are low cost, low risk and bought from a catalogue or common framework open to the whole public sector.
passages.anchor: Some suppliers may require no relationship management by an organisation when the goods, works or services are low cost and low risk

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 12, p.71
passages.text: This can be defined as the practices and behaviours adopted to engage more collaboratively with strategic suppliers to improve delivery of government objectives and increase mutual value beyond that originally contracted.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 12, p.69
passages.text: For complex projects the Playbook reports that a partnership model built on collaboration, openness, transparency and flexibility can help. Its critical success factors are a shared focus on service delivery, clear roles, a shared understanding of how disputes are resolved, and a collaborative culture.
passages.anchor: Critical success factors of a partnership model include

passages.locator: ISO 44001:2017 Collaborative business relationship management systems: concept only
passages.text: The ISO standard on collaborative business relationship management sets out a management system for collaborative business relationships between organisations, running from operational awareness and knowledge, through partner selection and working together, to value creation, staying together and exit strategy.

passages.locator: CIPS contract and supplier relationship management material: concept only
passages.text: Professional bodies such as CIPS teach contract management and supplier relationship management as separate but linked disciplines: the first protects what the contract promises, the second develops value with the suppliers that matter most.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.3 Managing delivery and performance
passages.text: Where performance is unlikely to, or does not meet the requirements of the contract, preventative and/or corrective action should be taken, within the terms of the contract, to remediate the situation, such as through formal notice or a performance improvement plan.

passages.locator: Contract Management Principles, principle 3
passages.text: Understand and use contractual options such as appointment of Remedial Advisor, Rectification Plans and Step In rights.

passages.locator: Procurement Act 2023, s.71(2)
passages.text: At least once in every period of twelve months during the life-cycle of the contract and on termination of the contract the contracting authority must

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Performance Notices (Procurement Act 2023), para 28
passages.text: When the contract performance notice is used to publish information about a supplier not performing a public contract to the authority’s satisfaction, the supplier must have been given proper opportunity to improve performance, and must have failed to do so before the notice is published.

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Performance Notices (Procurement Act 2023), para 26 and s.71(3)
passages.text: A breach triggers a contract performance notice only when it has led to partial termination, an award of damages, or a settlement agreement. A breach that ends in full termination is reported in the contract termination notice.
passages.anchor: partial termination of the contract (see paragraph 27 for publication requirements

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Performance Notices (Procurement Act 2023), para 34
passages.text: The contract performance notice must be published within 30 days of the day on which section 71(5) first applies in relation to a particular breach or failure to perform.

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Performance Notices (Procurement Act 2023), para 10
passages.text: A published performance notice creates a discretionary exclusion ground against the supplier in later procurements. The supplier is only at risk if the notice was published in the preceding 5 years and the circumstances are continuing or likely to recur.
passages.anchor: if the notice was published in the preceding 5 years

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Performance Notices (Procurement Act 2023), para 36
passages.text: For poor performance the clock starts when the authority decides the supplier has failed to improve after a proper opportunity. The guidance suggests this may be the date a notice was issued saying improvement had not happened, or that an agreed rectification plan had not been implemented.
passages.anchor: has failed to implement an agreed rectification plan

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Consulting Services: Unsatisfactory Performance, p.83
passages.text: Where a consultant's team performs poorly, the client uses the contract to ask for correction or replacement of staff. If the consultant fails to act, the client can move to further remedies under the contract, including termination or the dispute resolution provisions.
passages.anchor: If the consultant fails to take adequate corrective action/s

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Contractual Remedies, Figure XII, p.37
passages.text: World Bank guidance lists typical employer remedies under a works contract in rising order: a notice to correct a default, withholding payment, calling the performance security, delay damages for late completion, and termination when a contractual termination event occurs.
passages.anchor: Notification instructing a correction of default

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.5 Contract change control
passages.text: Contract changes shall be justified and controlled to ensure the requirements continue to meet the organisation’s business needs and align with the organisation’s financial processes

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.5 Contract change control
passages.text: The commercial functional standard expects change control to give an audit trail in a change register, a cost of change justified against the business case, approvals obtained before implementation, retained evidence for later procurement or disputes, and changes that are value for money and lawful.
passages.anchor: there is an audit trail of contractual changes defined in a change register

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), para 1
passages.text: If a modification cannot be justified on at least one of the grounds, the modification is not permitted and a new procurement must be carried out if the contracting authority wishes to implement the subject-matter of the modification.

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), table ground 1 (s.74(1)(b), s.74(3))
passages.text: A change is non-substantial under the UK Act if it does not lengthen or shorten the term by more than 10% of the maximum term provided at award, does not materially change the scope, and does not materially shift the economic balance in the supplier's favour.
passages.anchor: increase or decrease the term of the contract by more than 10% of the maximum term provided for on award

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), para 24 (s.74(4))
passages.text: A below-threshold modification may not move the estimated value by more than 10% for goods or services or 15% for works, and the total of all such modifications must stay below the threshold for that type of contract.
passages.anchor: increase or decrease the estimated value of the contract by more than 10% in case of a contract for goods or services or 15% in case of a contract for works

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), table ground 5 (Schedule 8, paragraph 4)
passages.text: A modification for unforeseeable circumstances is allowed when the circumstances could not reasonably have been foreseen before award, the overall nature of the contract stays the same, and the estimated value rises by no more than 50% (a cap that does not apply to utilities contracts).
passages.anchor: more than 50%. This 50% threshold does not apply if the contract is a utilities contract

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), para 15
passages.text: a contracting authority should not make repeated small below-threshold modifications to a contract in order to purchase additional goods, services or works when those modifications could reasonably have been made as a single (larger) modification

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), para 23
passages.text: The guidance gives examples of changes likely to tilt the economic balance toward the supplier: a modification lifting the supplier's profit from 8% to 16%, a transfer of valuable intellectual property to the supplier, or repeated additions that add up to a large volume of extra goods, services or works.
passages.anchor: increase in the supplier’s profit under the contract from 8% to 16%

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Modifications (Procurement Act 2023), para 8
passages.text: Where a change needs a contract change notice and the contract is worth more than £5 million including the change, the Act also requires publication of the modification or of the contract as modified, subject to listed exemptions.
passages.anchor: a value greater than £5 million (including the value of the modification itself)

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex II para 9.1(c), p.63
passages.text: For a contract subject to the Bank's prior review, the Borrower seeks the Bank's no objection before agreeing a variation or amendment that, alone or added to all earlier ones, adds more than 15 percent to what the contract first cost, extensions of time included; extreme urgency is the stated exception.
passages.anchor: any variation order or contract amendment (except in cases of extreme urgency), including due to extension of time, that singly or combined with all previous variation orders or amendments, increases the original contract amount by more than 15% (fifteen percent);

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Change Management Procedures, item 3, p.29
passages.text: The guidance asks for clear roles in change management, with named people holding delegated authority to act on a change request or to escalate it when there are problems.
passages.anchor: clarify who is responsible for what during change management, and ensure that individuals have clear delegated authority to act, or to escalate change requests where there are issues

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Cost Control, Figure VI, p.20
passages.text: When a contractor asks for a change order or variation, the World Bank guidance expects proper contractual justification, analysis, method statements and evidence of where the extra cost came from and why it is reasonable, and it expects the contract manager to track and control every increase that is granted.
passages.anchor: The contractor must provide proper contractual justification, analysis, method statements

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.53(3)
passages.text: issue a variation order requiring a contractor at his own expense to repair, replace, or to do anything in his or her contract left undone or found to have been carried out with inferior or defective materials or with less skill and expertise than required by the contract of award.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 11: Ongoing financial monitoring, p.65
passages.text: We shall therefore monitor the financial standing of our key suppliers on an ongoing basis.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 11: Resolution planning, p.64
passages.text: All new critical service contracts require resolution planning information from suppliers.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Introduction, definitions note 8, p.8
passages.text: Public sector dependent suppliers are supplier groups with over £50 million pa revenue of which over 50% is derived from public sector work.

passages.locator: Assessing and Monitoring the Economic and Financial Standing of Suppliers guidance note (2025), paras 4.2.1 to 4.2.2
passages.text: Key Suppliers are identified with the Contract Tiering Tool and include all suppliers of Gold (critical) and Silver (important) contracts. Their economic and financial standing should be reviewed at least once per year, and more often for critical suppliers or those with more than a low risk of failure.
passages.anchor: Suppliers should be reviewed at least once per year

passages.locator: Assessing and Monitoring the Economic and Financial Standing of Suppliers guidance note (2025), para 4.6.1 to 4.6.2
passages.text: Under the Model Services Contract, suppliers should promptly report a Financial Distress Event or anything that could cause one, and boards of suppliers of critical service contracts give an annual written confirmation. For works contracts and public sector dependent suppliers under closer monitoring, the guidance recommends that this confirmation be six monthly.
passages.anchor: it is recommended that confirmation by boards should be six monthly

passages.locator: Corporate Financial Distress guidance note (2025), section 2.4 Distressed organisation decline curve, p.8
passages.text: Financial decline can arise quickly, therefore an entity’s financial statements may not include signs of distress.

passages.locator: Corporate Financial Distress guidance note (2025), section 2.3.2 and Appendix 1
passages.text: Non-financial warning signs can show distress before published accounts do: requests to be paid in advance, invoice discounting or factoring, key supply chain partners refusing to keep trading, and suppliers seeking to renegotiate contract terms.
passages.anchor: Inability to retain supply chain members

passages.locator: Resolution Planning guidance note (May 2021), paras 1.4.1 to 1.4.4
passages.text: Resolution planning guidance applies to new critical service contracts, other outsourced service contracts worth more than £10m per year, and critical construction contracts. Such contracts should require the supplier to provide corporate resolution planning information and an insolvency continuity plan.
passages.anchor: with an estimated value exceeding £10m per year1; and Critical Construction Contracts.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.6 Contract risk management
passages.text: For critical public services organisations shall have resolution plans.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Managing Contract Risks, p.26
passages.text: The guidance expects the contract manager to review the risk register regularly while the contract runs, with input from the parties where that is appropriate.
passages.anchor: The Contract Manager should regularly review the risk register (with inputs, as appropriate, from the contracting parties) during contract implementation

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.2
passages.text: All regulatory authorities, operators, contractors, subcontractors, alliance partners and other entities involved in any project, operation, activity or transaction in the Nigerian oil and gas industry shall consider Nigerian content as an important element of their overall project development and management philosophy for project execution.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.3(1)
passages.text: Nigerian independent operators shall be given first consideration in the award of oil blocks, oil field licences, oil lifting licences and in all projects for which contract is to be awarded in the Nigerian oil and gas industry

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.6
passages.text: all subsequent oil and gas arrangements, agreements, contracts or memoranda of understanding relating to any operation or transaction in the Nigerian oil and gas industry shall be in conformity with the provisions of this Act.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.7
passages.text: In the bidding for any licence, permit or interest and before carrying out any project in the Nigerian oil and gas industry, an operator shall submit a Nigerian Content Plan ("the Plan") to the Board demonstrating compliance with the Nigerian content requirements of this Act.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, ss.8 and 9
passages.text: The Board reviews the Nigerian Content Plan and, if satisfied, issues a Certificate of Authorization for the project. Where it runs a public review of a plan, the review must be completed and the certificate issued or denied within 30 days from the start of the review.
passages.anchor: certificate issued or denied within 30 days from the date of commencement

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.10(1)
passages.text: (a) first consideration shall be given to services provided from within Nigeria and to goods manufactured in Nigeria; and (b) Nigerians shall be given first consideration for training and employment in the work programme for which the plan was submitted.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.11(3)
passages.text: All operators, alliance partners and contractors shall comply with the minimum Nigerian content for particular project item, service or product specification set out in the schedule to this Act

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.12
passages.text: setting out how the operator and their contractors will give first consideration to Nigerian goods and services, including specific examples showing how first consideration is considered and assessed by the operator in its evaluation of bids for goods and services required by the project.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.22(d) and (g)(iii)
passages.text: Before award, the operator gives the Board the selected contractor, designated sub-contractors, commencement and completion dates and, for construction or service contracts, the estimated Nigerian employment in person-hours, together with Nigerian content estimates for each bidder. These award-stage numbers become the baseline a contract manager later reports against.
passages.anchor: for construction or service contracts ; the estimated Nigerian employment (in person-hours)

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.24(1)
passages.text: The operator shall submit to the Board, within 30 days at the end of each quarter, a listing of all contracts, subcontracts and purchase orders exceeding $1,000,000 (USD) or such other limit as the Board may determine, awarded in the previous quarter.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.25
passages.text: before carrying out any work or activity in Nigeria, the operator or other body submitting a plan shall establish in the Catchment Area where the project is to be located, a project office where project management and procurement decision making are to take place

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.26
passages.text: The operator shall locate, within the project office, personnel with decision- making authority in accordance with a list of personnel to be approved by the Board.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.28(1)
passages.text: Nigerians shall be given the first consideration for employment and training in any project executed by any operator or project promoter in the Nigerian oil and gas industry.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.29(a) to (c)
passages.text: Every plan carries an Employment and Training Plan covering hiring and training needs of the operator and its major contractors, expected skill shortages, project specific training and forecast spend. The operator reports to the Board quarterly on employment and training against that plan, including new hires, their place of residence at hiring, and their employment status.
passages.anchor: report to the Board quarterly on employment and training activities for the reporting period

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.30
passages.text: Where Nigerians are not employed because of their lack of training, the operator shall ensure, to the satisfaction of the Board, that every reasonable effort is made within a reasonable time to supply such training locally or elsewhere

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.31(1)
passages.text: the operator shall submit to the Board a succession plan for any position not held by Nigerians and the plan shall provide for Nigerians to understudy each incumbent expatriate for a maximum period of four years and at the end of the four year period the position shall become Nigerianised.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.32
passages.text: For each of its operations, an operator or project promoter may retain a maximum of five per cent of management positions as may be approved by the Board as expatriate positions to take care of investor interests.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.33(1)
passages.text: the operators shall make application to, and receive the approval of, the Board before making any application for expatriate quota to the Ministry of Internal Affairs or any other agency or Ministry of the Federal Government.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.34
passages.text: all projects or contracts whose total budget exceeds $100 million (USD) shall contain a "Labour Clause" mandating the use of a minimum percentage of Nigerian labour in specific cadres as may be stipulated by the Board.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.35
passages.text: All operators and companies operating in the Nigerian oil and gas industry shall employ only Nigerians in their junior and intermediate cadre or any other corresponding grades designated by the operator or company.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.41(2)
passages.text: International or multinational companies working through their Nigerian subsidiaries shall demonstrate that a minimum of 50% of the equipment deployed for execution of work are owned by the Nigerian subsidiaries.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.44
passages.text: The operator shall submit to the Board annually a plan, satisfactory to the Board, setting out a programme of planned initiatives aimed at promoting the effective transfer of technologies from the operator and alliance partners to Nigerian individuals and companies.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.50
passages.text: No insurance risk in the Nigerian oil and gas industry shall be placed offshore without the written approval of the National Insurance Commission which shall ensure that Nigerian local capacity has been fully exhausted.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.51(1) and s.52(1)
passages.text: Operators, contractors and other entities in the industry must use Nigerian legal practitioners for legal services, and Nigerian financial institutions for financial services unless the Board accepts that this is impracticable. Operators file legal and financial services plans with the Board every six months.
passages.anchor: All operators shall submit to the Board, every six months, its Legal

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.52(3)(f)
passages.text: all operators, contractors and sub-contractors shall maintain a bank account in Nigeria in which it shall retain a minimum of 10 per cent of its total revenue accruing from its Nigerian operations.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.53
passages.text: all operators, project promoters, contractors and any other entity engaged in the Nigerian oil and gas industry shall carry out all fabrication and welding activities in the country.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.56
passages.text: The Joint Qualification System shall constitute an industry databank of available capabilities and shall be used for (a) sole system for Nigerian content registration and pre-qualification of contractors in the industry ;

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.60
passages.text: Within sixty days of the beginning of each year, each operator shall submit to the Board their annual Nigerian Content Performance Report covering all its projects and activities for the year under review.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.61
passages.text: The annual performance report sets out Nigerian content by category of spend on current and cumulative cost bases, with employment achievement as hours or days worked by Nigerian and foreign workers, and procurement achievement as quantity and tonnage of locally made and foreign materials.
passages.anchor: employment achievement in terms of hours or days worked by Nigerian and foreign workers

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.62
passages.text: The Board shall undertake regular assessment and verification of the Nigerian Content Performance Report filed by all operators

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.64
passages.text: all operators and contractors shall provide the Board or its designated agent with access to their facilities and all documentation and information required for substantiating the Nigerian content reported.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.65
passages.text: The operator shall ensure that its partners, contractors and subcontractors are contractually bound to report Nigerian content information to the operator and, if so requested by the Board, directly to the Board

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.66
passages.text: The operators shall effectively communicate its Nigerian content policies and procedures to its contractors and subcontractors and to monitor and enforce their compliance.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.68
passages.text: An operator, contractor or sub-contractor who carries out any project contrary to the provisions of this Act, commits an offence and is liable upon conviction to a fine of five per cent of the project sum for each project in which the offence is committed or cancellation of the project.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.104(2)
passages.text: The sum of one per cent of every contract awarded to any operator, contractor, subcontractor, alliance partner or any other entity involved in any project, operation, activity or transaction in the upstream sector of the Nigeria oil and gas industry shall be deducted at source and paid into the Fund.

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.106 (definition)
passages.text: "Nigerian Content" means the quantum of composite value added to or created in the Nigerian economy by a systematic development of capacity and capabilities through the deliberate utilization of Nigerian human, material resources and services in the Nigerian oil and gas industry;

passages.locator: NOGICD Act 2010, s.70(k)
passages.text: make auditing procedures and conduct regular audits for the purposes of monitoring and implementing compliances with the provisions of this Act;

passages.locator: NCDMB Guidelines for NCDMB Approvals of NOG Contracting Processes (2025), Purpose (vii) and Step 5, printed pp.10 and 25
passages.text: NCDMB's updated contracting-process guidelines add a Nigerian Content Compliance Commitment (NCCC) at award. It records the Nigerian content targets the operator and its contractor agree for the execution phase, and a Nigerian Content Compliance Certificate is issued by the Monitoring and Evaluation Directorate once the contract is performed and the commitments are met.
passages.anchor: upon performance of the contract and

passages.locator: NCDMB Guidelines for NCDMB Approvals of NOG Contracting Processes (2025), Purpose (vii)
passages.text: Describe the procedure for reviewing and approving of NCCC (containing details of Nigerian Content commitments to be achieved by the successful bidder during contract execution.

passages.locator: NCDMB Guidelines for NCDMB Approvals of NOG Contracting Processes (2025), Purpose (ii)
passages.text: The guidelines update the PCAD guidelines last issued in April 2018 to reflect the industry service level agreement of September 2023 and the Presidential Directives of February 2024, and they set out the roles of operators, service providers and NCDMB at each stage of tendering and contract execution.
passages.anchor: last reviewed and issued on the 16th of April 2018. ii. This update seeks to take cognizance of the recent developments in the oil and gas industry such as: a. Industry MOU/SLA endorsed by the Board, NNPC and IOCs in September 2023 September 2023. b. Three (3) Presidential Directives issued by the President of the Federal Republic in February 2024

passages.locator: NCDMB Guidelines for NCDMB Approvals of NOG Contracting Processes (2025), notes to NC Plan stage
passages.text: For a replacement contract, NCDMB asks for evidence that the prior contract met its Nigerian content commitments, such as the 1% Nigerian Content Development Fund remittance and the human capital development execution. Closing out one contract's commitments therefore affects the next award.
passages.anchor: Commitments such as NCDF 1% Remittance and NCDMB HCD Execution is

passages.locator: NCDMB Guidelines on the NOGIC Joint Qualification System, sections 1 and 2: concept only
passages.text: NCDMB's NOGIC JQS guideline makes the Joint Qualification System the single platform for contractor registration and pre-qualification, and also uses it for expatriate quota applications, Nigerian content compliance certificates, reports management and monitoring visits.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 3: Delivery model assessments, p.22
passages.text: A delivery model assessment (formerly known as a ‘make versus buy assessment’) is an analytical, evidenced-based approach to reach a recommendation on whether a contracting authority should deliver a service or part of a service in-house, procure from the market or adopt a hybrid solution.

passages.locator: Delivery model assessment guidance note (May 2021), para 2.2.1
passages.text: The delivery model guidance says the time needed depends on service complexity, data and resources, and gives 3-6 months as an indication for an initial assessment of mid-level complexity.
passages.anchor: it can take 3-6 months for an initial delivery model assessment of mid-level complexity

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Section V para 5.27
passages.text: The World Bank Regulations tie the choice of contract type and arrangement to what is being bought, how risky and complex it is, and value for money. Among the types they list are framework agreements, lump-sum and unit price contracts, time-based and performance-based contracts, turnkey contracts, and build-own-operate and build-operate-transfer arrangements.
passages.anchor: Framework Agreements, build-own-operate, and build-operate-transfer

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex V para 3.19(e)
passages.text: Among the contents of the procurement strategy, the Regulations list the contracting strategy: how the work is packaged and which types of contract are used.
passages.anchor: contracting strategy (contract packaging, types of contracts).

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex VIII paras 3.3, 3.7 and 3.13
passages.text: The World Bank matches contract type to what is known: lump sum where scope can be clearly specified and tied to milestones, unit price where the work is well defined but quantities are uncertain (as in roads or dams), and reimbursable cost for emergency repairs, with open records and cost-limiting incentives.
passages.anchor: as in roads or dams

passages.locator: Risk Allocation and Pricing Approaches guidance note (Jan 2026), Appendix II: Cost Plus, p.38
passages.text: Cost plus pays the supplier's allowable costs plus a margin and is described as particularly suited to novel or first generation contracts, where neither side can predict how the service or its cost will evolve. It demands open book transparency and a real effort to police allowable costs.
passages.anchor: particularly suited to novel or first generation contracts

passages.locator: Risk Allocation and Pricing Approaches guidance note (Jan 2026), Appendix II: Guaranteed Maximum Price with Target Cost, p.43
passages.text: Under a guaranteed maximum price with target cost, savings below target are shared, overruns above target are shared equally up to a cap, and the model services contract sets that cap 10% above the target price. It suits work where outputs are known but delivery methods are not yet fixed.
passages.anchor: (10% above target price in the model services contract)

passages.locator: Risk Allocation and Pricing Approaches guidance note (Jan 2026), para 6.1.6
passages.text: For contracts with considerable inflation uncertainty, using indexation is advisable.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Fixed Price Contracts and Inflation, p.24
passages.text: World Bank guidance records that price adjustment clauses are established practice for contracts running more than about 18 months, and recommends them for shorter contracts where inflation in key inputs is expected to be high.
passages.anchor: (normally exceeding 18 months)

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 7: Model Services Contract, p.48
passages.text: The Playbook recommends the Model Services Contract as a starting point and lists what users should tailor: performance indicators and service credits, insurance and parent company guarantees, invoicing and indexation, pricing, benchmarking, financial distress, and the governance and contract management structure.
passages.anchor: performance management: number and type of performance indicators, service credits and service points

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Works and Plant: Timely Notice and Submission, p.51
passages.text: The guidance stresses that a contractor gives notice of a claim and submits it on time, because a late notice or a late submission can carry consequences under the contract.
passages.anchor: Timely notice and timely submission of a claim by the contractor are essential as otherwise delayed notice and submission could have consequences based on the contract.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Works and Plant: Requirements for Contractor's Claims, p.51
passages.text: A claim, the guidance says, should state the breach of contract or the other legal basis it relies on.
passages.anchor: Claims should include statements of the contractual breach, or any other legal basis sought to be relied upon.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Works and Plant: Assessment of Claim, p.51
passages.text: In assessing a claim the contract manager checks three things: that the contract gives the contractor an entitlement to the time or cost claimed, that the extra time or cost was actually incurred and is reasonable in extent, and that the employer's default actually caused the loss claimed.
passages.anchor: that there is a cause and effect between the Employer’s default and the damages incurred by the contractor

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Works and Plant: Proof of Entitlement and Damages, p.51
passages.text: The guidance expects the contract manager to see that a claim is backed by an analysis of its costs and by documents such as invoices, reports and records.
passages.anchor: The Contract Manager is expected, as much as possible, to ensure that the contractor’s claim is substantiated by an analysis of costs and supporting documentary evidence such as invoices, reports and records etc.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Works and Plant: Analysis of Contractor's Billing, p.52
passages.text: With a claimed change, the first question is whether the so-called extra work was already in scope and has been mislabelled as extra. Only after that is settled are the costs checked for relevance and reasonableness, using contract unit rates first, then recorded historical costs, then market rates.
passages.anchor: check whether the claimed extra work is not an item which is contractually in-scope

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Contractor's Claims in Construction Contracts, p.50
passages.text: The World Bank guidance says good practice prevents many claims: understand the contract, pay on time, define scope and specifications properly, give timely access to site, and answer contractor notices on time.
passages.anchor: ensure timely responses to contractor’s notices

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Works and Plant: Determination of Costs, p.52
passages.text: For delay claims the contract manager tests idle labour and equipment (could they have been released or redeployed), unabsorbed site and head office overheads, and profit, checking whether the contract allows cost only or cost plus profit.
passages.anchor: allows cost compensation only or cost + profit

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Cost Control, p.20
passages.text: The guidance expects the contract manager to know in advance which costs, possible extra costs included, sit with the contractor and which sit elsewhere.
passages.anchor: The Contract Manager should have identified beforehand which types of cost (including any possible additional costs) are within the contractor’s responsibility and which are not.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Figure XIV, p.38
passages.text: The guidance lists what to record: how the supplier performed and delivered, every communication and notice, the dates, and who was involved.
passages.anchor: Keep records of performance, delivery, communications, notices, dates and the people involved.

passages.locator: FIDIC Conditions of Contract (Red Book and Silver Book, 2nd ed. 2017, reprinted 2022), claims and 'Agreement or Determination': concept only
passages.text: FIDIC conditions define what counts as a claim and set a notice and particulars procedure, and the Engineer (or the Employer's Representative in EPC forms) makes a fair determination of the matter under the contract. Course material describes these steps in its own words; the FIDIC clause text is licensed and is not reproduced.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Managing Contractual Disputes, p.35
passages.text: The guidance treats arbitration and litigation as the last resort for resolving a dispute.
passages.anchor: Arbitration and litigation should be considered as resolution methods of the last resort.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Dispute Management, p.36
passages.text: Depending on the contract, alternative dispute resolution may use an adjudicator, a dispute review expert or a dispute review board. The guidance stresses setting the mechanism up on time, since trying to create it after a dispute starts tends to fail.
passages.anchor: Trying to establish this mechanism after a dispute arises is a recipe for failure.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex IX paras 2.24 to 2.25
passages.text: For international competitive procurement the World Bank requires contracts to state the applicable law and forum, to include independent dispute resolution through Dispute Review Experts or Dispute Review Boards, and normally to provide international commercial arbitration in a neutral venue.
passages.anchor: Dispute Review Experts or Dispute Review Boards

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 6.3/6.4 (disputes)
passages.text: A process for handling and resolving commercial or legal disputes with suppliers should be defined and subject to governance controls in line with organisational policy.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.16(26)
passages.text: All procurement contracts shall contain provisions for arbitral proceedings as the primary forms of dispute resolution.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.1(1)
passages.text: The objective of this Part is to promote fair resolution of disputes by an impartial tribunal without unnecessary delay or expense.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.5(1)
passages.text: If a party sues on a matter covered by an arbitration agreement, the court must refer the parties to arbitration when a party asks no later than its first statement on the substance, unless the court finds the agreement void, inoperative or incapable of being performed.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.6(2)
passages.text: Where there is no agreement as to the number of arbitrators, the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.70(1) and (2)
passages.text: Where a contract requires mediation before court or other proceedings, the party concerned proposes a mediation agreement in writing. If no acceptance arrives within 30 days of sending the invitation, or any other time stated in it, the inviting party may treat the invitation as rejected.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.71(1)
passages.text: When the mediation proceedings commence, the running of the limitation period regarding the claim that is the subject matter of the mediation is suspended.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.76
passages.text: Unless the parties agree otherwise, everything about a mediation stays confidential, with exceptions for disclosure required by law, disclosure needed to implement or enforce the settlement, and disclosure needed to prevent or reveal a crime or a threat to a party.
passages.anchor: Unless otherwise agreed to by the parties, all information relating to the mediation

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.82(2)
passages.text: the settlement agreement resulting from the mediation is binding on the parties and enforceable in Court as a contract, consent judgment or consent award.

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.55(4)
passages.text: An application for setting aside shall not be made after three months have elapsed from the date on which the party making that application had received the award

passages.locator: Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (Nigeria), s.57(1) and (3)
passages.text: An arbitral award is recognised as binding whatever country it was made in and, on written application, the Court enforces it; with the Court's leave it may be enforced like a judgment or order.
passages.anchor: An award may, by leave of the Court, be enforced in the same manner as a judgment or

passages.locator: Procurement Act 2023, s.78(1)
passages.text: It is an implied term of every public contract that the contract can, if a termination ground applies, be terminated by the contracting authority in accordance with this section.

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Terminations (Procurement Act 2023), para 11 (s.78(2))
passages.text: The three implied termination grounds are: the contract was awarded or modified in material breach of the Act; the supplier has become excluded or excludable since award; or a sub-contractor is excluded or excludable.
passages.anchor: the contracting authority considers that the contract was awarded, or modified, in

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Terminations (Procurement Act 2023), para 15 (s.78(7))
passages.text: Before relying on the implied term, the authority must tell the supplier it intends to terminate, say which ground applies and why, and give the supplier a reasonable opportunity to respond.
passages.anchor: give the supplier reasonable opportunity to respond to the contracting authority on

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Terminations (Procurement Act 2023), para 18
passages.text: Contracting authorities should always set out in the contract what happens when the contract is terminated, including under the implied term in section 78.

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Terminations (Procurement Act 2023), para 18
passages.text: Practical termination terms to write into the contract include the notice period, transfer of assets and data, help with re-procurement, payment of sums owed, and any breakage costs for early termination.
passages.anchor: how long after serving notice the contract will terminate

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Terminations (Procurement Act 2023), para 26
passages.text: The notice must be published before the end of the period of 30 days beginning with the day on which the public contract is terminated (section 80(1)).

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.7 Contract transition and exit
passages.text: Early termination of a contract should be a last resort only enacted after other provisions for the delivery of the contract, including contractual remedies for improving performance, have been exhausted.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Contractual Remedies: Termination, p.38
passages.text: The guidance calls termination the ultimate remedy for a default.
passages.anchor: Termination of a contract is the ultimate remedy for default.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Figure XV case study, p.39
passages.text: In a World Bank case study an employer tried to terminate two slow road contracts after twelve months but found all earlier warnings to the contractor had been verbal. With no written record, termination was delayed by months.
passages.anchor: all previous notices to the contractor were verbal and there was no written documentation

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Figure XVI case study, p.40
passages.text: In another case study the employer's own late payments had forced the contractor to suspend work, so terminating for the contractor's abandonment was indefensible. The lesson: an employer must meet its own obligations, including timely payment, before relying on the contractor's default.
passages.anchor: Termination due to the alleged contractor’s default was indefensible.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Delay Damages, p.38
passages.text: Delay damages are deducted as a percentage or amount for late completion, usually with an aggregate limit (the guidance gives 10% of the contract price as an illustration). Reaching the limit usually permits termination, though continuing may still be the better option.
passages.anchor: (say, 10% of the contract price)

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 5: Protecting against supply chain risk, p.41
passages.text: These include step-in rights, the approval of key sub-contractors and assignment and novation provisions.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 11, p.64
passages.text: Departments are told to consult the Cabinet Office Markets and Suppliers team whenever they plan to terminate a service contract worth £5 million pa or more with a public sector dependent supplier.
passages.anchor: terminate a service contract worth £5 million pa or above with a public sector dependent supplier

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.53(4)
passages.text: Where the Bureau finds a contravention of the Act in procurement proceedings or contracts, its remedies include nullifying the proceedings, cancelling the procurement contract, ratifying what was done, or making a declaration.
passages.anchor: cancellation of the procurement contract

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex XI para 2.4, p.101
passages.text: The Regulations require an evaluation of how the contract was carried out, made at completion, to assess performance and, where it applies, to draw lessons for later contracts.
passages.anchor: An evaluation of the contract execution shall be carried out at the contract completion to assess the performance, and if applicable, identify any lessons learned for future contracts.

passages.locator: WB Procurement Regulations, 7th ed., Annex XI para 3.3(f), p.102
passages.text: Among the checks the Regulations list for value for money, the Borrower confirms that the final price of the contract compares well with comparable benchmarks.
passages.anchor: the final contract price compares favorably with comparable benchmarks.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Change Management Procedures, item 14, p.30
passages.text: At close-out the guidance asks for the changes made during the contract to be evaluated for their effect on cost, schedule and performance, and kept as lessons for the future.

passages.text: The guidance asks for the KPIs to be used in the review after the contract ends, and for the lessons to be recorded for future operations.

passages.text: Payment errors found before the final payment is made should be corrected, the guidance says.

passages.locator: GovS 008 v2.2, 5.4.7 Contract transition and exit
passages.text: On contract closure, information systems should be updated, staff and facilities (if any) reassigned and the contract documentation archived in accordance with the organisation’s information retention policy and procedures.

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 13, p.72
passages.text: Sufficient time should be allocated to knowledge transfer and lessons learned analysis. Did the KPIs drive the required behaviours and outcomes from the contract?

passages.locator: Sourcing Playbook (June 2023), Chapter 13, key point 2, p.73
passages.text: There should be sufficient means within the contract to incentivise the incumbent supplier to maintain both resources and performance up to the end of the contract.

passages.text: For the UK termination notice, 'termination' covers every way a contract ends: discharge (obligations fulfilled, payments made, disputes settled), expiry, termination by a party, rescission, or being set aside by a court.

passages.locator: Guidance: Contract Performance Notices (Procurement Act 2023), para 21

passages.locator: Contract Management Framework Summary, Area 11: Market Management, item 15
passages.text: Exit planning and a strategy for when the contract ends is put in place in a timely manner and includes input from the contract manager.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.57(2)
passages.text: The conduct of all persons involved with public procurement, whether as official of the Bureau, a procuring entity, supplier, contractor or service provider shall at all times be governed by principles of honesty, accountability, transparency, fairness and equity.

passages.text: Any person engaged in the public procurement and disposal of assets who has assumed or is about to assume, a financial or other business outside business relationship that might involve a conflict of interest, must immediately declare to the authorities any actual or potential interest.

passages.locator: Public Procurement Act 2007 (Nigeria), s.57(12)
passages.text: The Nigerian Act lists what counts as a conflict of interest, including a direct or indirect interest in or relationship with a supplier or contractor that could bring personal gain, taking personal advantage of an opportunity that belongs to the entity, and passing confidential information to a supplier or contractor.

passages.text: The Bank requires borrowers, bidders, consultants, contractors, suppliers, their sub-contractors and agents, and all of their personnel, to keep to the highest ethical standard through procurement, selection and the execution of Bank-financed contracts, and to refrain from fraud and corruption.

passages.text: The Regulations define a corrupt practice as offering, giving, receiving or soliciting anything of value, directly or indirectly, to influence another party's actions improperly.

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Fraud and Corruption, p.40

passages.locator: WB Contract Management Practice (June 2024), Fraud and Corruption, p.41
passages.text: Red flags of fraud and corruption during execution include poor quality materials or workmanship, change orders without contractual justification, unjustified changes in specification or conditions, payments that do not follow the contract, and false or duplicate invoices.

passages.locator: Guidance: Conflicts of Interest (Procurement Act 2023), para 2
passages.text: A conflict of interest arises in a procurement context where there is a conflict between the interests of a person acting in relation to a procurement and those of the procurement itself.
